text: A conveyor belt has packages with given weights. Every day you load the ship with packages from the belt, and you can't exceed the ship's capacity. Find the smallest capacity that gets everything shipped within days days.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I have to take the packages in belt order. I can't pick which ones go together. Is that right?

Good — I want to flag how much that one word is doing. Because the order is fixed, each day is just a contiguous run of the belt, so a shipping plan is really just where do I cut the sequence. If I were allowed to reorder, this would be bin packing, which is NP-hard. Small example: weights five, four, four, three with capacity eight. In belt order I get five, then four and four, then three — three days. If I could reorder, five and three, then four and four, is two. So belt order isn't decoration — it's what keeps this problem easy.
Also, a package can't be split across two days — it's all or nothing?
That pins down my lower bound, which I'll come back to. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to five times ten to the fourth packages, each weighing at most five hundred. And days is at most the number of packages.

So the total weight tops out around two and a half times ten to the seventh. That fits an int comfortably, so I don't need to worry about overflow here. Let me run through the example: weights one through ten, with five days. With capacity fifteen I get one through five, six and seven, then eight, nine and ten alone — exactly five days. With fourteen, the first day can only hold one through four, and I end up needing six. So fifteen is the answer.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to start at the smallest legal capacity and step up until one works. Correct, but capacities run to two and a half times ten to the seventh, and each test costs a pass over the belt. I could also compute the best cuts directly with dynamic programming, but at fifty thousand packages that's far too slow. This problem reminds me of searching on the answer. Computing the minimum capacity is hard, but checking one capacity is easy — walk the belt, start a new day when the next package doesn't fit, count days. And it's monotonic: a bigger ship never needs more days. So the capacities form a false, false, true, true pattern, and I want the first true. The hard optimization moves into the binary search, and the check stays a simple greedy.

Here's the plan. One: search capacities from the heaviest package up to the total weight. Two: a capacity fits if greedy packing in belt order needs at most days days. Three: if mid fits, keep it as the right end; otherwise move past it. One thing worth flagging — the lower bound is the heaviest package, not one. Below that, the heavy package never fits, but my greedy would still return a number — it just opens a new day and loads it anyway — so the check accepts an impossible capacity and I return something too small. And the greedy is optimal: pulling a package back into an earlier day that still has room keeps every day legal and never adds a day. The trade-off: each check is linear, over about twenty-five rounds. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main loop is the plan line for line, and getDay is the greedy, starting on day one with an empty ship. One thing worth flagging — curW plus-equals w sits outside the if on purpose. When I start a new day, the package that triggered the switch hasn't been loaded yet; it becomes the first item of the new day. Tucked into an else, that package would silently vanish and I'd undercount days. Two comparisons also matter. Inside, it's a strict greater than: filling the ship exactly is allowed. Outside, it's less than or equal: using every available day is allowed. Flipping either one pushes the answer the wrong way.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Weights one to ten, five days; the range starts at ten to fifty-five, and I expect fifteen. The deciding row is capacity fifteen: it uses all five days exactly, so the outer less than or equal keeps it. Fourteen and twelve both need six days, because the extra two units still can't fit the next package, a five. The day count is a staircase — monotonic, not strict, which is all binary search needs. It returns fifteen. That matches. Corner cases: three, two, two, four, one, four in three days gives six. One, two, three, one, one in four days gives three. Fifty thousand packages of five hundred in one day forces the total, twenty-five million; in fifty thousand days, it forces the max, five hundred.

The time complexity is n log of the total weight — roughly twenty-five rounds, each a fifty-thousand pass, so around a million operations. The space complexity is constant. In the worst case it's the same rule as any search on the answer: rounds times the cost of one check. Oh, one more thing — accumulate with a literal zero sums in int. That's fine here at two and a half times ten to the seventh, but if the weight limit ever grew, that line would be the first to overflow, and silently. Writing zero L L costs nothing. I also random-tested against a brute-force scan over capacities — two hundred thousand cases, no disagreement.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You showed why belt order matters by pricing out the alternative — bin packing, with a concrete reordering that beats the greedy. You argued the greedy check is optimal instead of just asserting it. And you explained the lower bound as a correctness issue, including the subtle part: an illegal capacity still returns a number, so it silently poisons the check. Good work.
